To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

myonuclei are added to muscle fibers when the fiber hypertrophies and that myonucleus number increases in response to both functional overload (FO), which causes muscle fiber hypertrophy, and GH/IGF administration.

functional overload combined with growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor I administration increased muscle and fiber size and myonuclear number in rat soleus muscles but did not affect the myonuclear domains of individual muscle fibers.

functional overload (FO), growth hormone (GH), and insulin-like growth factor I administration (IGF-I) each increased myonuclear number, but FO combined with GH/ IGF-I administration increased myonuclear domain volume.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that regulate muscle fiber size and composition.
understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms that regulate skeletal muscle mass and function.
the effects of growth factors on muscle growth and regeneration, with a particular interest in myonuclear domain regulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
myonuclear domain is maintained in rat soleus fibers after functional overload and growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor I treatment.
the myonuclear number is regulated to maintain the myonuclear density in a normal range.
myonuclear domain is not maintained in all circumstances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the myonuclear domains in the soleus are maintained when fibers are undergoing hypertrophy, whether it is due to FO or GH/IGF administration.
myonuclei are added to the muscle fibers in response to the hypertrophy of the fiber and that the myonuclear domains are maintained at a relatively constant size during fiber hypertrophy.
the myonuclear number is maintained during hypertrophy and that this is accomplished by a mechanism(s) that does not increase the domain size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
myonuclei can be added to the fiber in a manner that maintains the myosin protein per myonuclei ratio.
myonuclear domain remains the same in hypertrophying muscle, regardless of the mechanism by which the muscle grows.
the myonuclear number increases in proportion with fiber size, and this increase is not a result of myonuclear fusion or fission.
